creator: dailyhistoryclips
caption:
Glenn Gould was one of the great pianists of the twentieth century, and he sang while he played. Not quietly. A wordless humming that followed whatever line his hands were on, and it is there on almost every record he made.

Columbia’s engineers spent years trying to get rid of it. They pulled the microphones further from his face, changed the angles, tried putting a screen between him and the keyboard. Nothing worked. There was nowhere to put a microphone that could hear the piano but not the man bent over it.

Gould never treated it as a fault. He said he was not so much playing the music as thinking it, and the voice was part of the thinking.

He traced the habit back to his childhood, to an afternoon when the family vacuum cleaner was running while he practised. The noise swallowed the piano completely, and he realised he could hear the piece more clearly in his head than through his ears. He learned everything that way afterwards, away from the instrument, so by the time he sat down the music was already sounding inside him. The humming was just the overflow.

Put on his Goldberg Variations and there is a second instrument in the room, slightly out of tune with the first.

creator: thinkitthrough411
caption:
What could a second-century Buddhist philosopher possibly contribute to quantum mechanics?

Physicist Carlo Rovelli found a striking parallel between Nāgārjuna’s philosophy and his relational interpretation of quantum mechanics: things may not possess fully independent properties, but instead become what they are through relationships.

The resemblance does not mean ancient philosophy discovered modern physics—but it may offer physicists a different conceptual framework through which to understand it.

Follow @thinkitthrough411 for more!

#Nagarjuna #QuantumMechanics #Buddhism #Philosophy
transcript: The physicist Carlo Rovelli was developing an interpretation of quantum mechanics when people around him kept asking him whether he'd read a particular second century Buddhist philosopher. He finally did and he devoted an entire chapter of his book Helgeland to what he found. The philosopher was Nagarjuna and his Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way is one of the most rigorous works in the history of philosophy. Nagarjuna uses what could be interpreted today as a sort of four-valued logic, although this is contested. Namely that a thing is, is not, is both, or is neither, and then methodically dismantles every one of those options. His conclusion is that nothing possesses independent existence of its own. Instead everything is what it is only in relation to something else and he calls this aspect of reality emptiness. Now here's where Rovelli, a physicist, found that so striking. You see, Rovelli's relational interpretation of quantum mechanics holds that objects have no properties in isolation, only in relation to other objects. And so here were two thinkers, separated by 18 centuries and completely different methods, arriving at a structurally similar picture of reality. Rovelli said it helped him think more clearly about the physics, but he added something else. It also made him less anxious about impermanence, because it dissolved the permanent self he had been anxious about in the first place.

That's fine for phones and monitors, but it wastes a surprising amount of power. Our Sharp memory display works differently. Every pixel stores its own state, so once you draw something, it simply stays there. It's very similar to an e-paper screen. The display only needs a tiny maintenance signal in the background which makes it incredibly power efficient. Another thing I love is that it's reflective instead of backlit. So the brighter it is outside, the easier it is to read. Playdate, for example, uses a Sharp memory display and can run it up to 50 frames per second. That makes it a really interesting middle ground. You can get fast updates like a normal LCD, excellent outdoor visibility like e-paper, and low power consumption whenever the image is mostly static. We believe that’s about to change. Orbiter is our contribution toward making accurate 3D digitization as simple and practical as 3D printing is today. The project is open source. Let’s explore this field together, learn from each other, and see how far we can push this technology. Share your experiments, ideas, and improvements in the comments.

caption:
After testing this here are my main findings:
1. Really short emails get far more replies than long pitches. Try really hard to make it not read like AI. The best way to do this is to provide examples of exactly what the email should look like.
2. The fact that I have some followers on ig and TikTok definitely helped get replies lol. These journalists also want to be famous so framing it in a “I will get you more visibility” way certainly worked. 
3. AI is going to be bad at writing stories so actually try to put some work into ideation yourself. 
4. You apparently have to actually claim the Google profile thing. Mine hasn’t shown up yet so I haven’t gotten there yet. 
5. It is a volume game. You are competing with a ton of other people who want their attention too. 

I didn’t know a single thing about PR (other than some basic PR classes I took in college) but if you are good at sales most of the same principles seem to apply.

#ai #buildwithai #vibecoding #pr

creator: emils.salmins
caption:
This was my very first time making a hand-cut tile mosaic. Going in with a total DIY mindset, I originally thought it would take me two weeks max, but it ended up taking a full month to complete.
Specs-
Everything is hand-cut from 2x2 cm @winckelmans.1894 tiles using only two pliers: one from @speedball_art and a Leponitt Nipper.
I first glued the tiles onto a fiberglass mesh with Titebond glue. For the kitchen walls, I laid Knauf Aquapanels and mounted the mosaic using Mapei Adesilex P10 Tile Adhesive. I left the adhesive to cure for 30 hours before applying brown grout. Finally, because I left a 5 mm expansion gap between the tiles and surrounding surfaces all around the perimeter, I finished everything off with matching brown silicone.
